--- title: "What machine learning is" description: "How machine learning differs from the statistical modelling you already do, demonstrated on the same data, with the same question." order: 1 categories: [foundations] --- ## Starting from what you already do You already fit models. You have written a GLM, checked the residuals, looked at a coefficient and its confidence interval, and drawn a conclusion about how temperature affects abundance. So when a colleague suggests a random forest instead, the useful question is not "is machine learning better?" but "what is it *for*, and is that what I want?" This page answers that by doing the same thing twice. One dataset, one question, two approaches, and a result that is more interesting than "the new method wins". ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea A statistical model is usually built to **estimate something about the world**. You specify a form, say that abundance changes linearly with temperature, and the fitting procedure returns a number for that change, with an interval around it and a test of whether it differs from zero. The output is a *statement*: temperature is associated with an increase of so many individuals per degree, plus or minus. You can put it in a paper and someone can argue with it. A machine-learning model is usually built to **predict well on cases it has not seen**. You do not specify the form of the relationship; the algorithm searches for whatever shape fits, including shapes you would never have written down. The output is a *machine*: give it a new station's depth and temperature, and it returns an expected abundance. It generally cannot tell you why. Three practical differences follow. **Who chooses the form.** In a linear model, you do. That is a constraint, and constraints are how interpretation becomes possible: a single slope is meaningful precisely because you forced the relationship to be a single slope. Machine-learning methods relax the constraint and lose the interpretation along with it. **What counts as success.** Statistical modelling asks whether the estimated effect is distinguishable from noise. Machine learning asks how close the predictions land on data the model has never seen. A model can do well on one and badly on the other. **Where the honesty check sits.** In statistical modelling it is in the assumptions: residual plots, distributional checks. In machine learning it is almost entirely in holding data back, and measuring performance on the part the model never saw. That idea, the *test set*, runs through the whole course. ## Worked example Our stations record depth, temperature, chlorophyll, salinity and substrate, and the catch of one benthic species. We want to relate abundance to the environment. First, split the data. Three quarters to train on, one quarter held back and not looked at until the end. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate ``` ::: The statistical approach: a linear model, which returns coefficients. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lm_fit <- linear_reg() |> fit(predictors, data = train) tidy(lm_fit, conf.int = TRUE) |> select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| conf.low| conf.high| p.value| |:-----------------|--------:|--------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 27.975| -19.496| 75.446| 0.248| |depth_m | -0.017| -0.031| -0.002| 0.022| |temperature_c | -0.074| -0.217| 0.070| 0.314| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.029| 0.790| 1.269| 0.000| |salinity_psu | -0.706| -2.136| 0.725| 0.333| |substratemud | 1.280| 0.456| 2.105| 0.002| |substrategravel | 0.383| -0.656| 1.422| 0.469| |substraterock | -1.449| -2.898| 0.000| 0.050|
::: ::: Read that as you normally would. Chlorophyll has a clear positive association. Muddy stations hold more than sandy ones, rocky ones fewer. Salinity shows nothing: its interval comfortably spans zero. Depth declines significantly, if weakly. And temperature? An estimate of about $-0.07$ individuals per degree, an interval spanning zero, $p = 0.31$. On this evidence you would report that temperature shows no detectable association with abundance. Now the machine-learning approach. Same data, same variables, no specified form. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_fit <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") |> fit(predictors, data = train) rf_fit ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> parsnip model object #> #> Ranger result #> #> Call: #> ranger::ranger(x = maybe_data_frame(x), y = y, num.trees = ~500, seed = ~123, num.threads = 1, verbose = FALSE) #> #> Type: Regression #> Number of trees: 500 #> Sample size: 600 #> Number of independent variables: 5 #> Mtry: 2 #> Target node size: 5 #> Variable importance mode: none #> Splitrule: variance #> OOB prediction error (MSE): 20.37886 #> R squared (OOB): 0.1124542 ``` ::: ::: There are no coefficients to print. A forest of 500 trees has no single number describing what temperature does. What it has instead is predictions, so let us look at what it and the linear model have each concluded about temperature. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(train, aes(temperature_c, abundance)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, aes(colour = "What the linear model sees"), linewidth = 1.1) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.6, se = FALSE, aes(colour = "What is actually there"), linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("What the linear model sees" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], "What is actually there" = ml_palette[["blue"]])) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Abundance (individuals per station)", colour = NULL, title = "The linear model is not wrong about its line. Its line is wrong.") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Abundance against temperature in the training data. The straight line is the linear model's view; the curve is a flexible smoother. A straight line through a hump is flat, which is why the linear model reports no temperature effect.](what-is-machine-learning_files/figure-html/fig-temperature-1.png){#fig-temperature fig-alt='Scatter plot of abundance against temperature. Points form a hump peaking near 9 degrees. A nearly flat straight line runs through them, while a curved smoother rises to a peak at 9 degrees and falls away on both sides.' width=1400} ::: ::: The species has an optimum around 9 °C and thins out in colder and warmer water. The linear model was required to answer with a single slope. Averaged over a hump, the best straight line is nearly flat, so it reports, correctly and uselessly, that the slope is indistinguishable from zero. (The straight line above uses temperature on its own, while the coefficient table adjusts for the other variables, so the two are not numerically identical: one tilts very slightly up, the other very slightly down. Both are flat, which is the point.) The forest was never asked for a slope, so the hump costs it nothing. ## Reading the comparison Does the forest therefore predict better? Compare them on the held-back test set, and on the training data as well. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} performance <- function(fit, data, model) { augment(fit, data) |> rmse(truth = abundance, estimate = .pred) |> transmute(model, rmse = round(.estimate, 2)) } bind_rows( bind_cols(set = "Training", performance(lm_fit, train, "Linear regression")), bind_cols(set = "Training", performance(rf_fit, train, "Random forest")), bind_cols(set = "Test", performance(lm_fit, test, "Linear regression")), bind_cols(set = "Test", performance(rf_fit, test, "Random forest")) ) |> pivot_wider(names_from = set, values_from = rmse) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | Training| Test| |:-----------------|--------:|----:| |Linear regression | 4.35| 4.22| |Random forest | 2.09| 4.13|
::: ::: This is the interesting part, and it is not the tidy story you might expect. On the **training** data the forest looks twice as good, with a typical error of about two individuals against the linear model's four. On the **test** data, the data neither model has seen, the gap almost vanishes: roughly 4.1 against 4.2. Most of the forest's apparent advantage was not knowledge about the species. It was the forest memorising the particular stations it was trained on. This is **overfitting**, and it is so central that [section 5](../05-generalisation/index.qmd) is devoted to it. Note what caught it: the test set, and nothing else. Both models look fine on their own residuals. So the honest summary of this comparison is: - the forest understood the temperature relationship and the linear model did not; - the forest barely predicted better on new data; - only the linear model produced a number you could put in a paper. None of those three follows from the others. That is the whole point. ## Limits of this comparison **"Machine learning is more powerful" is not a general fact.** It is a claim about a specific dataset, and here it bought almost nothing. Flexible methods need enough data to pin down the shapes they are free to invent. With 600 noisy training rows, that freedom mostly bought memorisation. **Prediction accuracy is not understanding.** A model can predict well for reasons that have nothing to do with ecology. A habitat model can score highly by learning where the survey vessels went. [Section 10](../10-interpretation/index.qmd) deals with what you can honestly claim. **The linear model was not defeated, it was misused.** Given a quadratic term, or fitted as a GAM, it would have found the temperature optimum and still given you interpretable output. "Linear model" and "cannot bend" are not the same limitation. The real division is between *you specifying the form* and *the algorithm searching for it*. **Neither model can extrapolate.** Ask either about 22 °C water and you get an answer, confidently, from nothing. See [section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd). ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Statistical modelling estimates *something about the world*; machine learning builds *something that predicts*. They are different goals, not different quality tiers. - You choose the form in a statistical model. That constraint is what makes a coefficient interpretable, and what makes it wrong when the constraint is false. - A flat, non-significant coefficient can mean "no relationship" or "a relationship my model cannot express". They look identical in the output. - Performance on the training data tells you almost nothing. The held-back test set is the honesty check, and it is the reason to split your data before you start. - Flexible does not mean better. Here the forest fit the training data twice as well and predicted new data barely better at all. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add a quadratic temperature term to the linear model (`abundance ~ poly(temperature_c, 2) + ...`) and re-read the coefficients. Does the temperature effect become detectable? What does this say about reporting "no effect"? 2. Refit the forest with `trees = 5` instead of 500. Which changes more, the training error or the test error, and why?
